evidence.summary: The paper conducts a unified probe-based evaluation across eight encoder families (image-only self-supervision, video JEPA, video pixel MAE, latent action quantization, pixel diffusion, pixel reconstruction, shortcut-forcing dynamics, and Dreamer) on LIBERO, CALVIN, and MetaWorld. Section 6 Conclusion states: 'pixel-prediction quality and action recoverability are largely orthogonal: the standard metrics (PSNR, FVD, LPIPS) do not predict whether a representation encodes the underlying action. What matters is temporal predictive pretraining.' The inverse-dynamics loss 'acts as a multiplier that re-aligns structure already embedded by pretraining rather than manufacturing it' (Section 6). Appendix I (ID Supervision Sample-Budget Sweep) shows V-JEPA reaches high action-recovery even at sparse ID supervision levels while VideoMAE needs denser supervision, 'consistent with the view that V-JEPA's pretrained features already encode much of the action-relevant structure; ID supervision re-aligns rather than creates the signal.'
evidence.locator: Temporal predictive structure—not reconstruction fidelity—is the primary ingredient for action-relevant video world model representations. Self-supervised latent prediction (V-JEPA) achieves the best Pareto trade-off between visual fidelity and action prediction. ID supervision improves robustness to visual corruption but cannot create action-relevant structure absent from the backbone; it only re-aligns existing structure. Pixel reconstruction objectives (SDXL VAE, Cosmos) achieve highest PSNR but lowest action recoverability, demonstrating that pixel-level supervision can be counterproductive for action relevance.

claim: The field lacks a systematic understanding of when supervision signals (action labels, semantic annotations, geometric teachers) are necessary versus when self-supervised predictive objectives suffice; the survey maps the landscape across pretraining (predictive prior), joint training (integrated world-action models), post-training (data generation/simulation/reward), and inference, revealing that predictive fidelity and action utility frequently diverge.

evidence.summary: The survey organizes world models along three axes: representation (Section III), prediction-action interface (Section IV), and lifecycle stage (Section VI). Section II-C defines a world model as 'a predictive system, learned end-to-end or assembled from learned and analytic components' and distinguishes 'world-model objectives' (training signals like future-frame prediction or latent prediction) from deployed rollouts. Section VI-A (Pretraining) states: 'Predictive pretraining is attractive because robot interaction data are expensive, sparse rewards are difficult to obtain, and future prediction supplies dense supervision from trajectories that may not contain explicit task labels' but warns 'a model can learn visually or geometrically rich predictive features that transfer poorly to control if its pretraining objective does not preserve action consequences, contact structure, or embodiment-specific feasibility.' Section VI-B (Post-Training) notes world models can 'generate additional supervision, provide a learned environment for policy refinement, supply rewards or preferences, or filter hallucinated trajectories.' Section IV-A identifies that integrated prediction-action models 'avoid a brittle handoff between a world model and a separate executor' but suffer 'weaker causal accountability' since 'improved performance may reflect better representation learning rather than reliable predictive reasoning.' The Table in Section VI catalogs methods across stages: V-JEPA 2 (Pre/Infer, latent prediction), DreamerV3 (Train, latent rollout), GR-1/GR-2/WorldVLA (Train, joint world-action model), DreamGen (Post, data generation), WorldGym (Post, learned environment), NORA-1.5/SRPO/AtomVLA (Post, reward/preference scoring).
evidence.locator: The survey reveals a fundamental tension: 'predictive fidelity and action utility do not always coincide. A model may generate visually plausible futures while failing to preserve contact, object permanence, force closure, or action feasibility. Conversely, a compact latent model may support efficient control while hiding the physical structure needed for inspection, transfer, or safety-critical deployment.' The lifecycle perspective shows the same architecture needs different supervision at different stages: pretraining needs action-aligned predictive objectives, post-training needs hallucination-controlled simulation, and inference needs latency-bounded online correction. Open challenges include action alignment, hallucination control, contact modeling, and closed-loop benchmarking—none of which are resolved by pure end-to-end or pure supervised approaches alone.

claim: Self-guided world modeling—where future prediction targets are generated by the same policy pathway via EMA rather than external supervision—combined with frozen geometric teacher supervision, provides complementary benefits that improve manipulation performance without requiring separate pretraining or staged fine-tuning.

evidence.summary: Section 3.2 states SG-WAM uses 'two complementary designs: self-guided prediction models the action-conditioned evolution of policy-derived dynamics tokens using targets generated by the same policy pathway' and 'geometry supervision shapes the visual-token context.' Appendix D (Training Objectives) confirms: 'We train all online components jointly in a single-stage end-to-end optimization procedure... This joint optimization allows spatial supervision, action-conditioned future prediction, and action imitation to shape a common policy representation without requiring separate pretraining or stage-wise fine-tuning.' The ablation (Section 4.5, Table 4) shows: without either component = 95.3% avg; with both = 98.5%; removing world modeling drops 1.9pp; removing geometric supervision drops 0.9pp. The difference is most pronounced on LIBERO-Long (96.2% to 92.2% without WM). The frozen VGGT geometry teacher and EMA target pathway are removed at inference, leaving only the online VLM and action expert.
evidence.locator: Self-guided world modeling (where prediction targets come from the policy's own EMA pathway rather than external supervision) is effective for action generation, especially on long-horizon tasks requiring coherent state transition modeling. Geometric supervision from a frozen 3D teacher provides complementary spatial grounding. The key insight is that world modeling and action generation can share the same policy representation space without external future-state supervision, but geometric structure from a pre-trained 3D model still helps organize the representation around manipulation-relevant spatial relationships.

claim: Offline semantic mask supervision during training provides a geometric information bottleneck that produces more decision-relevant dynamics representations than raw RGB prediction, while the model operates purely on RGB at deployment without requiring semantic labels.

evidence.summary: Section 3.3 states: 'Offline semantic supervision; RGB-only at deployment. During training, each frame is paired with a semantic mask for task-relevant entities (robot arm/gripper and manipulated objects). These masks are used only to supervise the backbone predictor; at deployment, the model takes only raw RGB as input.' Section 5 (Conclusion) confirms: 'MWM uses semantic supervision only offline during training, while operating purely on raw multi-view RGB at test time.' The paper compares three variants (Section 4): MWM-C1 (explicit future-mask decoding with inverse dynamics model), MWM-C2 (predictive latent features with action diffusion head, without explicit mask decoding), and full MWM (end-to-end mask world model). Section 3.1 motivates the approach: 'By predicting future semantic masks, MWM introduces a geometric bottleneck that preserves decision-critical structure while filtering out irrelevant photometric variation.' The robustness analysis (Section 4.3) shows MWM achieves higher nPAUC than GE-ACT (0.648 vs 0.629) under random token pruning, attributed to the semantic bottleneck concentrating capacity on object geometry.
evidence.locator: Semantic supervision acts as an information bottleneck that filters photometric nuisance variables (texture, illumination, background) while preserving decision-critical structure (object identity, spatial layout, contact dynamics). The key design choice is that supervision is needed only during training—the deployed model is RGB-only. This demonstrates that targeted supervision (semantic masks) can shape representations that are more robust and generalizable than those learned from RGB prediction alone, but the supervision need not persist at inference.

claim: Disentangling dynamics learning from visual synthesis into a two-stage pipeline (low-resolution dynamics preview + high-resolution refinement) is more effective than monolithic end-to-end video generation for producing action-relevant world models, because accurate dynamics modeling requires low-level temporal reasoning that is not necessarily learned in high-resolution settings.

evidence.summary: Section 1 (Introduction) identifies the core problem: 'dynamics modeling is tightly entangled with high-fidelity visual synthesis' and 'accurate dynamics modeling requires low-level temporal reasoning to produce smooth transitions such as contacts, slips, and occlusions, which concentrates on physical interaction patterns and is not necessarily learned in high-resolution settings with redundant textures.' Section 3.4 describes the training: 'We train the full system in two stages for stability. We first train the world model alone using the objectives in Eq. 4, obtaining a reliable video predictor. Afterwards, we attach the action expert and optimize it on demonstrations while jointly fine-tuning the world model... The gradients from the imitation learning loss propagate through both the action generation expert and the world model.' The ablation (Section 4.3, Table 3) shows: full two-stage DVG-WM achieves FVD 152.36; single-stage 'Only Preview' gets 238.72; 'Only Refine' gets 169.29; '360p Preview + Refine' gets 188.47; 'Naive Cascading' gets 187.69. Real-world results show DVG-WM achieves 62.2% average success vs CogVideoX's 34.0% (28.2% improvement).
evidence.locator: The paper demonstrates that separating dynamics learning (low-resolution, contact-focused) from visual synthesis (high-resolution, texture-focused) produces better world models than entangling both in a single end-to-end objective. The disentangled design allows dynamics to be learned efficiently at low resolution where physical interaction patterns dominate, then refined with minimal computation. This challenges the pure end-to-end paradigm by showing that architectural decomposition (not just supervision) can improve both prediction quality and downstream action planning. However, the world model itself is trained without action supervision—it uses language conditioning only.

claim: External representation supervision (REPA with DINOv2, VideoMAEv2, DepthAnything3, V-JEPA2) brings little improvement or even degrades performance for video world models, while self-supervised representation shaping within the model's own latent space (future-predictive supervision on intermediate layers, cross-modal alignment, hard-negative repulsion) is more effective and adds negligible overhead.

evidence.summary: Section 1 (Introduction) identifies the core problem: 'in the unified WAM paradigm... both the Video DiT and the Action DiT are supervised only at their outputs—the former by a future-video generation loss and the latter by a trajectory planning loss. The intermediate representations... are thus never directly optimized; they emerge only as byproducts of fitting the final outputs.' Section 4.3 (Comparison of Representation Learning Methods) provides the key evidence: 'methods without external representations yield only modest gains over Vanilla Flow, while ReWorld attains the lowest FVD by a clear margin. More strikingly, methods that rely on external representations, including REPA variants driven by DINOv2, VideoMAEv2, DepthAnything3, V-JEPA2 and ReDi, bring little improvement and in several cases perform worse than the baseline.' The paper explains: 'their feature spaces are not always optimized to preserve fine-grained temporal evolution, precise geometry, and agent dynamics. This limitation also highlights the advantage of self-supervised representation learning within the generative model itself: ReWorld supervises intermediate features entirely in the video model's own representation space and optimizes them directly for future prediction.' Results: FVD reduced from 81.3 to 61.9 (23.9%), convergence accelerated ~2x, PDMS improved from 89.1 to 90.4 'without any post-training such as RL or post-processing.'
evidence.locator: The paper provides the first controlled comparison of representation learning methods for video world models, revealing that external supervision from pre-trained vision models (DINOv2, VideoMAEv2, V-JEPA2, DepthAnything3) transfers poorly to long-horizon driving video generation—sometimes performing worse than no representation guidance at all. Self-supervised shaping within the model's own latent space is superior because the representation is optimized directly for the world modeling task rather than for generic visual understanding. This directly challenges the assumption that external pre-trained features necessarily improve world model training, and supports the view that end-to-end self-supervised objectives can be more effective than externally supervised representation alignment.
